subject: physics

items.q: Which statement describes a scalar quantity?
items.correct: It is described by a magnitude only, and never by a direction.
items.misconception: It is described by a magnitude and also by a direction.
items.why: Scalar and vector are unfamiliar technical words met as a pair, with no everyday meaning to anchor which is which, so students learn the two definitions correctly but attach them to the wrong names. Anchor the words. A vector is drawn as an arrow, and an arrow points somewhere, so a vector needs a magnitude and a direction. A scalar just 'scales' — it is a size alone, like a mass of 5 kg or a speed of 30 m/s, with no direction attached.
items.random_wrong: It is a quantity that does not describe anything moving.

items.q: Which statement is true of a vector quantity but not of a scalar quantity?
items.correct: It has a direction associated with its magnitude.
items.misconception: It can be given a size in a unit such as the newton.
items.why: Numerical answers are rewarded in most calculations, so students learn to stop once a number and a unit have been written down. Check every force answer for two parts. If the answer would be equally true for a push to the left and a push to the right, the direction is still missing.
items.random_wrong: It always describes an object that is moving.

items.q: Two forces are drawn as arrows on the same diagram. One arrow is twice as long as the other. What does this tell you?
items.correct: The force shown by the longer arrow is twice as large.
items.misconception: The two forces are equal, but drawn at two different scales.
items.why: In sketches used in other subjects an arrow is purely a pointer, and students carry that habit into physics diagrams where the arrow is a scale representation. Read a force arrow as carrying two pieces of information at once. Drawing a 20 N force twice as long as a 10 N force is not decoration; it is the part of the diagram that records the magnitude.
items.random_wrong: The longer arrow was drawn bigger just to look neat.

items.q: Which statement best describes what a force is?
items.correct: A push or pull on an object due to another object.
items.misconception: A property of an object that heavy objects have more of.
items.why: Everyday phrases such as 'the force of the blow' or 'it has a lot of force' treat force as a substance an object carries, rather than as an interaction between two objects. Always finish the sentence: which other object is exerting this force? If no second object can be named, what is being described is not a force.
items.random_wrong: Something stored in a moving object and used up later.

items.q: A crate is dragged across a rough floor. Why is the friction between the crate and the floor a contact force?
items.correct: Because the crate and the floor are physically touching.
items.misconception: Because the crate stays right next to the floor below.
items.why: Students classify by what is visible around the object rather than by which two objects the force acts between. Because a falling ball touches air, it looks as though contact is involved. Name the two objects the force acts between first, then ask whether those two objects are touching. For weight the pair is the Earth and the object, and they are physically separated.
items.random_wrong: Because the crate is also touching the air around it.

items.q: The Earth pulls on a satellite high above its surface. Why is this gravitational force a non-contact force?
items.correct: Because the Earth and the satellite are physically separated.
items.misconception: Because there is no air in space to pass the force along.
items.why: Students classify by what is visible around the object rather than by which two objects the force acts between. Because a falling ball touches air, it looks as though contact is involved. Name the two objects the force acts between first, then ask whether those two objects are touching. For weight the pair is the Earth and the object, and they are physically separated.
items.random_wrong: Because the two objects can never touch one another.

items.q: Which of these is an example of a contact force?
items.correct: The tension in a stretched tow-rope
items.misconception: The magnetic force between two bar magnets
items.why: The classification is read off the final position of the objects rather than off the nature of the force, and a magnet held against a fridge does touch it. Ask whether the force can act with a gap between the objects. Magnetic, electrostatic and gravitational forces all can, so they are non-contact forces however close the objects end up.
items.random_wrong: The gravitational force on a falling ball

items.q: Which of these is an example of a non-contact force?
items.correct: The electrostatic force between charges
items.misconception: The air resistance on a falling skydiver
items.why: Air is invisible and is not thought of as an object, so students judge the skydiver to be touching nothing at all. Treat air as matter that can be touched. Contact with the particles of the air is real contact, which is why the specification lists air resistance among the contact forces.
items.random_wrong: The upthrust on a boat floating on the sea.

items.q: Which pair of forces are both non-contact forces?
items.correct: Magnetic and gravitational forces
items.misconception: Air resistance and electrostatic force
items.why: Air is invisible and is not thought of as an object, so students judge the skydiver to be touching nothing at all. Treat air as matter that can be touched. Contact with the particles of the air is real contact, which is why the specification lists air resistance among the contact forces.
items.random_wrong: Drag in water and the magnetic force.

items.q: A student writes that the force on a trolley is 12 N. Why is this description incomplete?
items.correct: Because force is a vector, so a direction is needed.
items.misconception: Because the mass in kilograms was not given too.
items.why: Everyday language calls the reading on kitchen scales a weight, and those scales are marked in kilograms, so the two quantities arrive already merged. Keep the units apart and the quantities stay apart: mass, m, in kilograms, kg; weight, W, in newtons, N. Weight is a force and mass is not.
items.random_wrong: Because a force in newtons must be converted to kilograms.

items.q: A tennis ball is struck by a racket. Which statement describes the interaction between them correctly?
items.correct: Each exerts a force on the other, equal in size and opposite in direction.
items.misconception: Only the racket exerts a force, because it moved first of all.
items.why: The damage to the two vehicles is very different, and students reasonably read the unequal damage as evidence of unequal forces rather than of unequal mass. Separate the force from its effect. The forces of an interaction pair are equal in magnitude; the car is damaged more because the same size of force acts on a much smaller mass.
items.random_wrong: The racket pushes the ball harder than the ball pushes the racket.

items.q: Which statement about the weight of a book resting on a shelf is correct?
items.correct: It is the force acting on the book due to gravity.
items.misconception: It is the total amount of matter contained in the book.
items.why: Everyday language calls the reading on kitchen scales a weight, and those scales are marked in kilograms, so the two quantities arrive already merged. Keep the units apart and the quantities stay apart: mass, m, in kilograms, kg; weight, W, in newtons, N. Weight is a force and mass is not.
items.random_wrong: It is the push of the shelf upwards on the book.

items.q: An astronaut takes a 3 kg toolbox from the Earth (g = 9.8 N/kg) to the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg). What happens?
items.correct: Its mass stays at 3 kg but its weight becomes smaller.
items.misconception: Its mass and weight both fall, because gravity is weaker there.
items.why: Because mass and weight are already confused, anything that reduces one is assumed to reduce the other, and 'less gravity on the Moon' is a familiar fact. Work through W = m g. Moving the toolbox changes g only. The m in the equation is the same number on the Moon as on the Earth, so only W changes.
items.random_wrong: Its mass and weight both drop to about a sixth.

items.q: Which equation is used to calculate the weight of an object?
items.correct: weight = mass × gravitational field strength
items.misconception: weight = mass ÷ the gravitational field strength
items.why: The equation is remembered as a string of symbols rather than as a relationship, so the operation written in it is repeated whichever quantity is being found. Rearrange before substituting. Start from W = m g, isolate the quantity asked for, and only then put the numbers in; a mass in kilograms should come out smaller than the weight in newtons wherever g is greater than 1 N/kg.
items.random_wrong: weight = mass plus gravitational field strength

items.q: A rock has a mass of 12 kg. The gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg. What is the weight of the rock?
items.why: 'Directly proportional' is read as a vague statement that one quantity increases with the other, rather than as a fixed multiplying relationship. Test proportionality with a ratio, not a difference. If W ÷ m gives the same value for every object in the same field, the two quantities are directly proportional, and the graph is a straight line through the origin.

items.q: A bag has a weight of 49 N at a place where the gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg. What is the mass of the bag?
items.correct: 5 kg
items.why: The equation is remembered as a string of symbols rather than as a relationship, so the operation written in it is repeated whichever quantity is being found. Rearrange before substituting. Start from W = m g, isolate the quantity asked for, and only then put the numbers in; a mass in kilograms should come out smaller than the weight in newtons wherever g is greater than 1 N/kg.

items.q: Which row gives the correct units for the quantities in W = m g?
items.correct: W in newtons, m in kilograms and g in newtons per kilogram
items.misconception: W in kilograms, m in kilograms and g in newtons per kilogram
items.why: Everyday language calls the reading on kitchen scales a weight, and those scales are marked in kilograms, so the two quantities arrive already merged. Keep the units apart and the quantities stay apart: mass, m, in kilograms, kg; weight, W, in newtons, N. Weight is a force and mass is not.
items.random_wrong: W in grams, m in kilograms and g in newtons per kilogram

items.q: What does g stand for in the equation W = m g, and what is its unit?
items.correct: Gravitational field strength, measured in newtons per kilogram
items.misconception: The force of gravity acting on the object, given in newtons
items.why: The symbol g is spoken aloud as 'gravity', and a quantity that appears in a force equation is assumed to be a force itself. Read the unit. N/kg means newtons per kilogram of mass, so g tells you how much weight each kilogram gets. The force itself is W, the answer, not g.
items.random_wrong: The weight of the object, measured in kilograms.

items.q: Why is the weight of an object drawn as a single arrow from one point on it?
items.correct: Because the weight may be taken to act at the centre of mass.
items.misconception: Because weight acts where the object presses on the surface below.
items.why: The visible effect of weight is felt at the surface an object rests on, so students place the force there instead of at the centre of mass. Distinguish the two forces at a contact. The push on the ground is the contact force between the object and the surface; the weight is the pull of gravity on the whole object, drawn from its centre of mass.
items.random_wrong: Because gravity only acts on the part touching the ground.

items.q: The weight of an object and the mass of an object are directly proportional. What does this mean?
items.correct: Doubling the mass doubles the weight in the same field.
items.misconception: Weight increases by a fixed amount each time mass increases.
items.why: 'Directly proportional' is read as a vague statement that one quantity increases with the other, rather than as a fixed multiplying relationship. Test proportionality with a ratio, not a difference. If W ÷ m gives the same value for every object in the same field, the two quantities are directly proportional, and the graph is a straight line through the origin.
items.random_wrong: Weight just gets bigger by some amount when mass increases.

items.q: A block of mass 4 kg has a weight of 24 N on a planet. A second block on the same planet has a mass of 12 kg. What is its weight?
items.correct: 72 N, because the mass is three times larger and so the weight is too.
items.misconception: 32 N, because the extra 8 kg of mass adds another 8 N to the weight.
items.why: 'Directly proportional' is read as a vague statement that one quantity increases with the other, rather than as a fixed multiplying relationship. Test proportionality with a ratio, not a difference. If W ÷ m gives the same value for every object in the same field, the two quantities are directly proportional, and the graph is a straight line through the origin.
items.random_wrong: 2 N, because the mass is divided by the gravitational field strength.

items.q: Which instrument is used to measure the weight of an object?
items.correct: A spring-balance calibrated in newtons
items.misconception: A set of kitchen scales marked in kilograms
items.why: The instrument is used in lessons about mass and weight together, and any device that something is hung from is assumed to give a mass reading. Look at the scale on the instrument. A newtonmeter is marked in newtons because the spring responds to the force pulling on it, which is the weight of the object hung from it.
items.random_wrong: An electronic balance reading in kilograms

items.q: What is meant by the resultant force on an object?
items.correct: The single force with the same effect as all of them together.
items.misconception: The largest of all of the forces that are acting on the object.
items.why: Tug-of-war language, in which the stronger side wins, encourages the idea that the smaller force is beaten rather than that it reduces the overall effect. Replace 'wins' with 'reduces'. The smaller force takes away from the larger one, so the single force with the same effect is smaller than the larger force acting alone.
items.random_wrong: The force that is left once the object has stopped moving.

items.q: A box is pulled to the right with a force of 12 N while a friction force of 5 N acts to the left. What is the resultant force?
items.correct: 7 N acting to the right
items.misconception: 17 N, acting to the right
items.why: Resultant is remembered as 'add the forces up', and the arithmetic is done on the magnitudes without the directions being considered. Take direction into account before adding. Choose one direction as positive, give the opposing force a negative sign, and add; the resultant then carries both a magnitude and a direction.
items.random_wrong: 12 N acting to the right

items.q: A ball hangs at rest on the end of a string. A free body diagram of the ball is drawn. Which forces should appear on it?
items.correct: The weight of the ball and the tension in the string, both acting on the ball.
items.misconception: The tension in the string and the pull of the ball on the string as well.
items.why: Interaction pairs are learned as forces that go together, so students draw both members of each pair even though only one of them acts on the isolated object. Isolate the object first. A free body diagram shows one object with only the forces acting on it; the partner force of each pair acts on something else and belongs on that object's diagram.
items.random_wrong: The weight of the ball and the pull of the ball on the Earth below.

items.q: A parachutist falls at a steady speed. Her weight is 700 N. What can be said about the forces on her?
items.correct: Air resistance is 700 N upwards, so the resultant force is zero.
items.misconception: The forces cancel out, so really no force acts at all.
items.why: 'No resultant force' is heard as 'no force', so students conclude that the individual forces must have switched off rather than combined to zero. Keep the forces and their combined effect separate. Each force is still there and still drawn on the free body diagram; it is only their total effect that is zero.
items.random_wrong: Her weight and the air resistance are an action pair.

items.q: A single force is resolved into two components acting at right angles to each other. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The two components together have the same effect as the force.
items.misconception: The two components add up numerically to the size of the single force.
items.why: Resolving is treated as splitting a quantity like a length of string, so the magnitudes are expected to share out arithmetically. Remember that components act in different directions, so their magnitudes cannot simply be added. Drawn to scale, components of 3 N and 4 N at right angles replace a single force of 5 N, not 7 N.
items.random_wrong: Each component is exactly half the size of the original single force.

items.q: Two forces at right angles act on a point. A student draws them to scale, head to tail, to find the resultant. What must the final answer state?
items.correct: The magnitude in newtons and the direction of the force.
items.misconception: The magnitude in newtons only, since that is the number asked for.
items.why: Practice with forces in a straight line lets a bare number stand as a complete answer, and the habit survives into vector diagram work where it no longer does. Force is a vector, so an answer without a direction is incomplete. A scale drawing supplies both parts: measure the arrow for the magnitude and the angle for the direction.
items.random_wrong: The direction only, because a scale drawing cannot give a size.

items.q: Is speed a vector quantity because a moving object is always going somewhere?
items.correct: Speed is a scalar: it has magnitude only. Velocity is the vector, because velocity states a speed together with a direction.
items.misconception: Any quantity that describes something moving must be a vector, so speed counts as a vector.
items.why: Motion feels directional, so students attach direction to every quantity that describes it. The pair speed/velocity is also used interchangeably in everyday speech, which hides the distinction the specification draws. Test the quantity, not the situation: ask whether the number alone fully describes it. '30 m/s' is a complete speed but an incomplete velocity, because a velocity is not fixed until a direction such as 'north' is added.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If the forces in an interaction pair are equal and opposite, why does anything ever move?
items.correct: The two forces act on two different objects, so they can never cancel each other out. Only forces acting on the same object combine to give a resultant.
items.misconception: The two forces of an interaction pair act on the same object, so they always cancel and nothing can accelerate.
items.why: Balanced forces on one object and the two forces of an interaction pair look identical when drawn as a pair of opposing arrows, and students merge the two ideas. Label every arrow with the object it acts on. An interaction pair always has one arrow on each of the two objects; balanced forces always have both arrows on the same object.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A bag weighs 49 N where g = 9.8 N/kg. To find its mass, does it matter whether you work out 49 ÷ 9.8 or 9.8 ÷ 49?
items.correct: Yes. Mass = weight ÷ g, so it must be 49 ÷ 9.8 = 5 kg. Division order matters: 9.8 ÷ 49 = 0.2, which is not the mass.
items.misconception: Division can be done in either order, so you just divide one of the two numbers by the other and it makes no difference which goes on top.
items.why: Multiplication is commutative and students carry that property over to division; a calculator accepts the numbers in whichever order they appear in the question, so the reversed division goes unnoticed. Order matters in division. Rearranging W = m g gives mass = W ÷ g, so the weight goes on top: 49 ÷ 9.8 = 5 kg. A sense check catches the reversal: a bag weighing 49 N — about five bags of sugar — cannot have a mass of only 0.2 kg.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.5.1 Forces and their interactions
